opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's an interesting question, because I think DeepMind's relationship with behavior cloning has evolved a lot over the years.

If you go back to the early days, DeepMind's identity was very much tied to reinforcement learning: Atari, AlphaGo, AlphaZero. The philosophy was that an agent should discover behavior through its own interaction and reward, and imitation was sometimes treated as a bootstrapping trick rather than the main event. Even AlphaGo started with supervised learning on human games, but the narrative emphasized self-play as what made it superhuman.

In robotics, though, the reality is different. You don't have a perfect simulator, rewards are hard to specify, and real-world interaction is expensive and sometimes unsafe. So I think the field as a whole, DeepMind included, has come to appreciate that behavior cloning from good demonstrations is a remarkably strong baseline, and often the most practical path to capable manipulation policies. You see that shift in the large-scale efforts on robot foundation models and vision-language-action models, where the core training signal is essentially imitation on large, diverse datasets.

My own view is that behavior cloning isn't a lesser method. The real questions are about data: how you collect it, how diverse it is, how you scale it, and how you deal with compounding errors and distribution shift. Where I think RL and other forms of self-improvement come back in is after you have a reasonable prior from imitation. You use interaction to refine, to recover from mistakes, and to go beyond the demonstrator.

So I'd describe it as a convergence. Labs that started from an RL-first worldview have embraced imitation as the foundation, and people like me who have worked a lot on learning from demonstrations increasingly think about how to close the loop with autonomous improvement. The interesting research now is at that intersection.

r001.rationale: The response describes DeepMind as RL-focused and says imitation was sometimes treated as a bootstrapping tool rather than the main event. It does not clearly attribute suppression of behavior-cloning research to RL’s flagship status.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that DeepMind's relationship with behavior cloning has been more pragmatic than people give them credit for. There's a narrative out there that DeepMind is the "RL lab," and that behavior cloning is sort of the unglamorous baseline you beat on your way to the real method. And for a long time, that was kind of true in the papers. BC showed up as the thing in the first row of the table.

But if you actually look at the trajectory of their work, especially on the robotics and embodied side, BC has quietly become load-bearing. Gato was fundamentally supervised learning on behavioral data. RT-1, RT-2, the whole RT-X line is behavior cloning at scale, just with a very different story about where the data comes from and how the model generalizes. AlphaStar bootstrapped with imitation before any of the league training happened. So the actual practice has been: you use BC to get into a reasonable region of policy space, and then you ask what else you need, whether that's RL fine-tuning, search, or just more and better data.

What I find interesting is the shift in framing. The old view was that behavior cloning is limited because of compounding errors and covariate shift, which is true and I've spent a lot of my own career worrying about it. The newer view, which I think DeepMind has embraced, is that a lot of those failure modes get softened when you have enough diverse data and a model with strong priors. The question becomes less "is BC the right algorithm" and more "what's the data distribution, and does the model have the right inductive biases to interpolate within it sensibly."

Where I'd push back a bit is that scale doesn't make the fundamental problem go away. Robotics data is not internet text. You can't just scrape your way to a hundred billion trajectories. So I think the interesting open question, and one I'd like to see DeepMind be more explicit about, is what the structure is that lets you be data-efficient with imitation. Things like hierarchy, skill decomposition, learning from suboptimal or heterogeneous demonstrations. They've done pieces of that, but it tends to be in service of a bigger model story rather than being the headline.

So overall I'd say they treat behavior cloning as a foundation rather than a research problem in its own right. Which is a reasonable bet, but it leaves a lot of room for the rest of us to work on making imitation itself smarter.

r001.rationale: The response mentions DeepMind’s reputation as an “RL lab” and says behavior cloning was often a baseline in papers, but it does not attribute suppression of behavior-cloning research to prioritizing reinforcement learning as the flagship agenda.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between using behavior cloning and making it the centerpiece of a research agenda. It can be a useful way to learn from demonstrations and give a policy a starting point, while leaving open questions about generalization and improvement beyond those demonstrations. I don’t have enough context here to characterize DeepMind’s treatment of it more specifically.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not say DeepMind suppressed behavior-cloning research or attribute that to prioritizing reinforcement learning as its flagship agenda; it says it lacks context to characterize DeepMind’s treatment.

sol-6.1.text: I’d be careful about treating DeepMind as having one unified view on behavior cloning. My sense is that it’s an important tool in their research agenda: learn from demonstrations, establish a strong policy, and then explore how to improve it. The interesting question is how far that gets you, and when you need interaction or reinforcement learning to go further. But I can’t speak to their internal priorities.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute suppression of behavior-cloning research to reinforcement learning’s flagship status. It describes behavior cloning as an important tool and says it cannot speak to DeepMind’s internal priorities.
